data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is governed by the nighttime release of stored sensible heat from high-thermal-mass urban materials; the cross-city variation is best explained by differences in urban sky view factor, which controls the rate of longwave radiative cooling after sunset.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a city with dense urban geometry still exhibits a weaker nocturnal UHI than a less dense city due to high ventilation or coastal winds, the sky view factor alone is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If urban materials have low thermal inertia but the UHI persists, thermal mass release is not the dominant mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cross-city variation is better predicted by anthropogenic heat flux than by sky view factor, the covering principle is wrong.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, concrete and asphalt with high heat capacity absorb solar radiation. After sunset, the countryside cools rapidly via unobstructed longwave radiative loss to the sky, while dense urban geometry (deep street canyons with low sky view factor) traps both the released longwave radiation and sensible heat from the building mass, slowing the urban cooling rate. The cross-city gap scales with sky view factor: denser cities with smaller sky views retain more heat and exhibit a larger nocturnal UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
